name: Hadrian’s Wall
summary: The north-west frontier of the Roman empire for nearly 300 years: a wall 80 Roman miles long from the Tyne to the Solway, built by the army on Hadrian’s orders after his visit in AD 122, with forts, milecastles and turrets. It was given up about AD 142 when the frontier moved north to the Antonine Wall, and reoccupied some twenty years later.
uncertainty: Course: drawn through the positions of the sixteen forts from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway, placed from general knowledge, so the line cuts corners between forts by up to a kilometre. The whole wall lies inside the map. The Antonine Wall (Forth–Clyde, about AD 142-160) lies just outside the map’s northern edge and is not drawn. The break in use about 142-160 is not shown. The end date is nominal: garrisons stayed into the early 5th century and some forts were occupied later.

name: Military Way (Hadrian’s Wall)
summary: The road added behind Hadrian’s Wall when it was recommissioned about AD 160, linking the forts and milecastles.
uncertainty: Course: the fort positions of the Wall shifted about 300 m south so that the road shows as its own line; the real road ran between the Wall and the Vallum, usually within 50-100 m of the Wall. English Heritage says only that a road was added when the Wall was brought back into use; the year is approximate.

name: Offa’s Dyke
summary: A bank up to 2.5 m high with a ditch on the Welsh side, the longest earthwork in Britain, marking the western edge of Mercia. Asser, writing about 893, credits it to King Offa (757-796); English Heritage places the work in the 780s.
uncertainty: Course: a generalised line of the near-continuous central section from Rushock Hill near Kington to Treuddyn in Flintshire, drawn from general knowledge of its route and accurate to perhaps a kilometre. Short gaps, including the stretch along the Severn near Buttington, are drawn through. Dating is debated: radiocarbon samples from under the bank at Chirk (2014) gave dates between about AD 430 and 652, which may mean parts are older than Offa; the Offa’s Dyke Association summarises recent scientific dates as provisionally late 8th to early 9th century. Earlier writers took it on to the sea at Prestatyn; the earthworks north of Treuddyn are now usually treated as separate. The year shown is nominal.

name: Offa’s Dyke (lower Wye section)

uncertainty: Course: generalised from general knowledge. Whether these earthworks are part of Offa’s work, or a separate and possibly different-dated boundary, is disputed; between here and Rushock Hill, across Herefordshire, there are only short isolated lengths, which are not drawn.

name: Wat’s Dyke
summary: A bank with a ditch on its west side, running about 60 km from Basingwerk on the Dee estuary south past Wrexham and Oswestry to the river Morda at Maesbury, a few kilometres east of Offa’s Dyke.
uncertainty: Course: generalised from general knowledge of its route through Hope, Wrexham, Ruabon and Old Oswestry. Its date is unsettled: a radiocarbon date from Maes-y-Clawdd near Oswestry gives only ‘after AD 486±75’, which led some to place it in the 5th century, while luminescence dates from Gobowen point to the early 9th century, the reading followed here. It may be earlier or later than Offa’s Dyke.

uncertainty: Course: generalised from general knowledge. Its date is not established: it is later than the Roman road it cuts and is usually placed in the 5th or 6th century as a British or early West Saxon frontier work, but a later Saxon date has been argued. The year shown is nominal. No source was fetched for this entry (Historic England’s list entries could not be retrieved).

name: The Ridgeway
summary: The chalk ridge route from the Avebury area along the Berkshire Downs to the Thames at Goring, and on along the Chiltern scarp (as the Icknield Way) to Ivinghoe Beacon, passing Barbury, Uffington and Segsbury hillforts. National Trails describe it as in use for at least 5,000 years.
uncertainty: Course: the modern National Trail, drawn through its main landmarks from general knowledge. That a single long-distance prehistoric road existed here is an old idea that archaeologists now doubt: the monuments along the ridge are real, but a continuous through-route is not evidenced before the early medieval period, when Anglo-Saxon charters name it. The start date is nominal.

name: Great North Road (London–York–Berwick)
summary: The main medieval road from London to the north, by Barnet, Hatfield, Baldock, Stamford, Grantham, Newark, Doncaster, Boroughbridge, Durham and Newcastle to Berwick, with York reached by a branch from near Wetherby or Ferrybridge. Kings and armies used it throughout the Scottish wars.
uncertainty: Course: straight segments between the towns on the route, placed from general knowledge; no source was fetched. The name is post-medieval. In the Middle Ages the route out of London by Ware, Royston and Huntingdon (the Old North Road, on Roman Ermine Street) was at least as important as the Barnet line drawn here, and the two joined near Alconbury. The start date is nominal: the route took shape gradually as the towns on it grew in the 12th and 13th centuries.

name: England–Wales border
summary: The boundary between Wales and England as fixed by the Laws in Wales Acts of 1535-6 and 1542-3, which assigned each marcher lordship to a Welsh or an English county. It runs from the Dee estuary to the Severn, near but seldom on Offa’s Dyke.
uncertainty: Course: the modern boundary, extracted from Office for National Statistics county boundaries (2025) as the edge shared by Welsh and English counties, simplified to 64 vertices; the estuary ends and the lowest part of the Wye are added by hand. The modern line differs from that of 1536-43 only in small later adjustments, which are not shown. Monmouthshire is treated as Welsh: the 1542-3 act left its status ambiguous and it was often counted with England until the 20th century.
